Senses.Explanation: A phonetic borrowing for the formal code of precepts. The term occurs 42 times in 30 allowlisted texts. The Chan corpus does not leave the borrowing unexplained: the Collection for Resolving Doubts in the Chan School gives the direct formula, 'the code of precepts is precisely these precepts,' after quoting the Buddha's instruction to rely on it as teacher after his death. The Revised Baizhang Code repeats that instruction, while a preface to a monastic code calls the code of precepts the sage's life and says the Baizhang regulations arose from it. The term also enters the teaching seat. Shiyu raises the whisk, asks whether the assembly understands, and says, 'This is the code of precepts,' before repeating that buddhas and the present teacher bind it in this way. In another interview a novice calls every precept code 'sand in the eye,' and the master replies, 'I do not believe you yet.' The Zen-specific deployment therefore places the inherited code at the stated root of Chan institutional regulations and makes it an object of public presentation and testing, rather than an outside specialist concern.
Senses.Note: The Sanskrit cross-reference is retained only as an alternate searchable label; the preferred English translates the corpus function.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Chan polemical collection quotes the posthumous-teacher formula and immediately glosses the borrowing as these precepts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝等比丘於我滅後。當尊波羅提木叉。是汝大師。如我住世無異也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Revised Baizhang Code preserves the instruction to honor the precept code as teacher.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “when hunger comes, eat rice.” Zen records turn this ordinary act into a compact answer, appraisal, and recurring line, most often paired with “when tired, sleep” (困來眠／困來打睡). Lingzhao answers her family's hard/easy exchange, “neither hard nor easy: when hungry, eat rice; when tired, sleep” (也不難，也不易，飢來喫飯，困來睡). Yuanwu places the line directly after “understand that ordinary mind is the Way” (了取平常心是道，饑來喫飯困來眠). One Dongshan teacher says he does not know how to discuss Chan or speak of the Way and “only, when hungry, eats rice; when tired, sleeps” (祇是饑來喫飯，困來打睡). Dazhu Huihai's recorded exchange supplies the crucial contrast: asked whether everyone does the same, he says no, because “when they eat, they refuse simply to eat and make a hundred demands; when they sleep, they refuse simply to sleep and make ten thousand calculations” (他喫飯時不肯喫飯，百種須索；睡時不肯睡，萬般計較). Other records caution that merely repeating the line as if already finished may still be “not yet” (未在), and one later speaker calls it only “one flavor of the ordinary” and not yet the monk's further matter. The entry therefore records both its elevated interview use and the corpus's own refusal to make parroting it sufficient.
Senses.Note: #0g deviation: common eating becomes a stock Chan answer and self-description paired with sleeping, while the records themselves distinguish the phrase from merely behaving ordinarily or repeating a slogan. The graph-variant spelling “when hungry, eat rice” (饑來喫飯) is more frequent than the headword spelling (飢來喫飯): the headword has 93 hits in 53 texts and the variant has 193 hits in 107 texts. The exact line “when hungry, eat rice; when tired, sleep” with the graph for “hungry” (飢) has 12 hits in 11 texts. The target keeps “eat rice” (喫飯) concrete as eating rice or a meal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 凡夫見拄杖，喚作拄杖；聲聞人見拄杖，認得箇頑空，撥無拄杖；菩薩人見拄杖，豈曾挂著齒牙？飢來喫飯，困來打睡，寒來向火，熱則取凉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A four-part ordinary-action series follows contrasting responses to a staff: eat when hungry, sleep when tired, approach fire when cold, take coolness when hot.

Occurrences.Kwic: 了取平常心是道。饑來喫飯困來眠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's record directly couples the line with “understand that ordinary mind is the Way.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山不會談禪，不會說道，祇是饑來喫飯，困來打睡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Dongshan teacher's self-description: he cannot discuss Chan or speak of the Way; he only eats when hungry and sleeps when tired.

Occurrences.Kwic: 他喫飯時不肯喫飯，百種須索；睡時不肯睡，萬般計較，所以不同也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dazhu's explicit contrast explaining why his eating and sleeping are not simply the same as everyone's.
